### Agent setup: skills, profiles, and hooks Installation also equips supported coding agents to use the graph in daily work. The native `install` command detects clients and installs the integration pieces their documented formats support: | Component | What it adds | |-----------|--------------| | **MCP configuration** | Connects the client to the local server and its tools. | | **Instructions and skills** | Explains graph-first exploration, index freshness, coverage checks, and when to read source. | | **Scout, Verify, and Auditor profiles** | Offers fast provisional lookup, task-directed verification, or bounded full verification, where custom agents are supported. | | **Session and compaction hooks** | Restores graph context at supported lifecycle events. | | **Search and read hooks** | Adds relevant graph context to supported searches and flags recorded coverage gaps after supported file reads. | Hook augmentation is context-only and fail-open: it does not replace or block the requested tool call. Features vary by client and platform; some clients use durable instructions or a parent-agent handoff instead of hooks or direct subagent MCP access. Codex users review and trust installed hooks through `/hooks`. See [Multi-Agent Support](#multi-agent-support) and [Sessions, compaction, and subagents](#sessions-compaction-and-subagents) for exact support and activation requirements. Hooks are enabled by default. Run `codebase-memory-mcp install --no-hooks` to remove CBM-managed hooks while keeping MCP registration and other integration files; the choice persists for later installs and updates. Run `codebase-memory-mcp install --hooks` to re-enable them, or inspect the current preference with `codebase-memory-mcp config get install_hooks`. ### Session Coordination Daemon CBM automatically shares one per-account coordination daemon across Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and every other configured client. There is no opt-in setting for MCP servers or hook clients: the first daemon-backed CBM session starts it, each session registers its own work, and a session-managed daemon stops after the final session. A daemon started with `daemon start` remains running until stopped. The daemon owns long-lived background services such as watchers, shared indexing jobs, and the optional UI. Closing one session cancels work owned only by that session, while work still needed by another session continues. The detached daemon does not depend on an MCP frontend's stderr. It keeps owner-only durable records under the canonical `${CBM_CACHE_DIR}/logs` directory (default `~/.cache/codebase-memory-mcp/logs`): | File | Contents | |------|----------| | `cbm-daemon.log` | Daemon lifecycle, watcher/indexing, UI, resource, and error events. | | `daemon-conflicts.ndjson` | Exact-build, coordination-ABI, and cache-root admission conflicts. | | `activation-events.ndjson` | Install/update/uninstall activation progress and outcomes. | Thin frontends still write immediate startup and session-specific errors to their own stderr; MCP JSON-RPC stdout remains clean. All active CBM processes must run the exact same version, executable build, coordination ABI, and canonical cache root. Equivalent `CBM_CACHE_DIR` aliases resolve to the same root; a genuinely different root is rejected while any CBM process is active. MCP servers, hooks, one-shot CLI commands, temporary index workers, and the daemon share a crash-safe OS admission barrier; starting an ordinary conflicting process fails before doing work and records an explicit conflict in `${CBM_CACHE_DIR}/logs/daemon-conflicts.ndjson`. The native `install` and `uninstall` commands are the deliberate exception to that conflict rule. For installation, download, verification, and private same-filesystem staging finish before activation so a bad candidate never disrupts active work. The native `update` command prints the installer command that performs the update. Activation then publishes account-wide maintenance intent, asks the daemon and every temporary local operation to cancel, and waits to a finite deadline for all coordinated CBM processes to exit. It holds the admission and lifetime barriers exclusively while changing the active binary, configuration, PATH, or indexes. New CBM work cannot enter during this window. Activation progress and results are recorded in `${CBM_CACHE_DIR}/logs/activation-events.ndjson`, and a successful command tells you to restart open coding-agent sessions so they launch the activated build. Package-manager setup (npm, PyPI, or Go) verifies and caches the native executable for that package. It does not replace the active native installation and therefore does not stop running CBM sessions. When that cached binary is executed, it still enters the same exact-build admission barrier. The shell and PowerShell installers invoke the verified candidate's native `install` command, so they do receive the full account-wide activation guarantee. The ordinary `cli` mode runs one command locally, but it is not disconnected from the daemon above: it connects to the shared coordination daemon (starting one if none is already running) for that same admission barrier plus per-project locks on graph mutations. Its connection is a `cli_session`: it does not register a project watcher or open a browser, and it holds the admission lease only for the command's lifetime. The shared daemon may serve Lens according to its UI configuration and available assets. If the command's own connection is what started the daemon, that daemon exits again once the command closes and no other session is attached; if a daemon was already running, the command simply joins and leaves it exactly as found. While the command is running, a temporary monitor separately lets activation cancel that operation and its supervised worker safely; the monitor exits with the command and never becomes a standing daemon. See [CLI Mode](#cli-mode) for details. ### CBM Lens Beta: code visualization and source navigation **CBM Lens is an optional visual companion to the MCP server, currently in open beta (v0.0.1).** Standard native releases include its browser interface, so you can launch Lens directly after installation; UI-enabled source builds include it too. It builds on [CodeAtlasWeb](graph-ui/README.md) by [Bernhard Jackiewicz](https://github.com/BernhardJackiewicz) (design and tracking in #1964). Lens is served on loopback. Browser AI downloads its optional model only after you enable it; inference stays on-device. Each panel names where its facts come from, and what the index did not record is shown as a gap. Start the local server: ```bash codebase-memory-mcp daemon start --open --port=9749 ``` The browser opens at `http://127.0.0.1:9749`. A permanent daemon keeps the UI available after the command exits. Use `daemon status` to inspect it and `daemon stop` when you are finished. For an MCP session, `--ui=true --port=9749` enables the same shared UI. Active clients must use the same executable build and cache directory. **Open your first repository** 1. Open the project menu and choose **Add project index**. You can also use `Alt+P`. 2. Choose a local repository folder and name the index. Files stay in place. 3. Start indexing and follow its reported status. You can close the dialog while it runs and reopen its activity from the project menu. 4. Open the indexed project. Start with Architecture for an overview or Explore to read a file. To bookmark a view, use `?project=&workspace=architecture`. Other workspace values are `explore`, `galaxy`, `adr`, `coverage`, and `system`. | Workspace | What you can do | |-----------|-----------------| | **Explore** | Navigate the indexed file tree and read source in Monaco. File impact shows what depends on the open file; Code details shows the callers, calls, references and related tests of the symbol under the caret. | | **Galaxy** | Search and focus graph nodes, load their neighbors layer by layer, switch to hierarchy, follow a path, and open source. Back and Forward return to earlier views. The coverage shadow marks known gaps around the loaded graph. | | **Architecture** | Explore the folder map, entry points, routes, hotspots, system structure, and behavior paths. Select a node or connection to inspect its evidence. | | **ADR** | Read and edit the project's architecture decision record. Save explicitly; the document is stored with the index and shared with `manage_adr`. | | **Coverage** | Check indexed, partially parsed, skipped, and excluded paths, together with available freshness information. | | **System** | Inspect daemon activity, indexes, and logs. Filter logs by project, severity, or text. | **Architecture views** - **Overview:** move through source folders and files on a 3D map. Choose source-size or uniform height, language or kind colors, and relationship filters. Switch to Entry points to follow a static call graph from a starting symbol. - **Routes:** switch between the service map and endpoint connections. Deployment metadata and indexed route evidence are shown separately; unresolved registrations remain visible. - **Hotspots:** inspect symbols using measured signals such as fan-in and complexity. Gravity wells help locate frequently referenced areas. They are not a code-quality score. - **System structure:** inspect component dependencies, expand groups, isolate cycles, and follow connections back to source evidence. - **Behavior:** choose a source and a reachable destination to inspect static call paths and their source statements. These paths show possible relationships, not a recorded execution order. Runtime observations require separately ingested traces. Drag a 3D view to orbit, scroll to zoom, and select a node or edge to inspect it. Edge colors distinguish relationships, and pulses indicate their direction. Reduced-motion preferences pause the pulses. Large views show their limits and omitted counts. A missing edge can reflect an indexing or display limit, so check Coverage and the source before drawing conclusions. #### Chat with your codebase locally Open **Chat** with the panel button at the top right to ask about the code you are looking at. In Explore it uses the open file or the exact text you have selected; in Galaxy it uses the selected node and its loaded neighbors. You can also attach graph evidence through **Add context**. 1. Click the robot icon at the top right to open the agent configuration. 2. Choose a local model. The default Qwen2.5 Coder 0.5B downloads about 567 MB; Qwen3 0.6B, LFM2.5 1.2B and Qwen3.5 2B are larger options. All need WebGPU with `shader-f16` support. 3. Click **Download & load**. Select a smaller range when you want to focus the answer. When you select a symbol, the chat lists its indexed facts and the lines of its code, and the model adds one sentence; that sentence is left out when it claims something the source does not show. The chat history is kept for 24 hours in this browser, per project. If a prompt is too long for the model, older messages are left out first; if it still does not fit, CBM Lens asks you to select less code instead of cutting the code. This chat explains the context you give it; it cannot edit files or run tools. Check its answers against the source. For callers and callees, ask in the chat; the answer is listed from the graph. **Architecture decisions** The ADR workspace keeps an unsaved draft per project in this browser tab. It checks whether the stored document changed before saving, but the API does not provide an atomic document lock. The editor accepts up to 8,000 UTF-8 bytes. Saving changes the indexed decision document, not a file in your repository.
Experimental agent activity The Agents workspace and activity overlays are hidden in normal builds. To include them in a source build: ```bash VITE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENTS=true scripts/build.sh --with-ui ``` Activity comes from explicitly configured tool hooks. The bundled adapter supports Claude Code PostToolUse; other clients need their own adapter. Recorded events go to the local daemon, and the reader must enable activity before the browser polls them. This does not automatically observe every agent. See the [frontend setup guide](graph-ui/README.md#experimental-agent-activity).
For troubleshooting, open System logs. Frontend errors and failed requests are recorded locally. `GET /api/ui-log` reads frontend entries from the daemon's SQLite journal; `${CBM_CACHE_DIR}/logs/ui.log` is also retained as a rotating JSONL export. See the [frontend README](graph-ui/README.md) for log scope, model setup, and development details. ### Auto-Index Enable automatic indexing on MCP session start: ```bash codebase-memory-mcp config set auto_index true ``` `auto_index` is off by default. When enabled, new projects are indexed automatically on first connection. The configurable file limit is `config set auto_index_limit 50000`. Previously indexed projects can be watched through `auto_watch` (on by default), subject to its global setting and session ownership. Each initialized, long-lived MCP session can register its root project when it connects and any target from a successful `index_repository` call, including custom project names and roots in another worktree. While `auto_watch` is enabled, these watches belong to the registering sessions and remain while at least one owning session is connected; closing the last owner removes the watch. Under a daemon started with `daemon start` a watch outlives its last owning session: the project stays watched and is re-indexed in the background when it changes, until that daemon stops, the project is deleted, its directory disappears, or `auto_watch` is set to `false`. An async index registers its target only after success and while its requesting session remains connected. CLI indexing and failed MCP indexes do not register watches. Global `auto_watch` controls registration and removes all watches on the next refresh or registration request when set to `false`. `index_status` reports this in its `watch` object: `watched`, and either the poll cadence and last scan time or the `reason` it is not watched. Watcher registration is controlled globally by `auto_watch` (default `true`). On the next refresh or registration request, `true` allows MCP sessions to register their root on connect and their successful `index_repository` targets; `false` removes all watches. CLI indexing and failed MCP indexes do not add watches. To turn the watcher off entirely, set `config set watcher_enabled false` (default `true`): the background poll thread never starts and no project is registered, while `auto_index` and manual `index_repository` keep working. Unlike `auto_watch`, which takes effect on the next refresh or registration request, `watcher_enabled` is read once when the background daemon starts, so run `codebase-memory-mcp daemon stop` after changing it; reconnecting your MCP client alone will not restart the daemon. See [docs/CONFIGURATION.md](docs/CONFIGURATION.md#2-cli-managed-runtime-settings). The watcher follows **git** projects only by default: a project indexed from a directory that is not a git repository is not watched and stays at its last index until you run `index_repository` again. To have such roots polled too, set `config set watch_non_git true` (default `false`, read when the daemon starts): they are then checked on the same cadence with a file-tree scan that uses the indexer's own ignore rules. Linked git worktrees are indexed as their own projects by default. Set `config set ignore_worktrees true` to skip them on the automatic paths — useful when short-lived `git worktree add` checkouts would otherwise each leave behind a permanent index of the same repository. An explicit `index_repository` call on a worktree is then refused unless you pass `index_worktree=true`. See [docs/CONFIGURATION.md](docs/CONFIGURATION.md#ignore_worktrees). ### Keeping Up to Date **Updates run from the install script on every platform, not from inside the running binary.** `codebase-memory-mcp update` validates your flags and then prints the exact command to run: ```bash # macOS / Linux bash "/install.sh" ``` ```powershell # Windows powershell -File "\install.ps1" ``` The install script is placed next to the binary at install time, so the printed path resolves beside the executable. It is idempotent, so re-running it *is* the update: it stops the daemon, retires the running binary, installs the new one, and cleans up. Why it works this way. On Windows it is a hard requirement; a running executable cannot replace its own image, so the swap has to happen from a process that is not the binary being replaced. On macOS and Linux it is a deliberate choice: an in-process updater is structurally a downloader (fetch an archive, verify it, unpack it, mark a file executable, run it), and shipping that composite in every binary to serve a command most people run a handful of times is a poor trade. The release archives now carry no download URLs at all, and **cbm makes no network request of its own accord**: it does not check for new versions in the background, and nothing phones home. You find out about releases from the install script, your package manager, or GitHub. If PowerShell refuses to run the script because the file came from the internet, `Unblock-File` it first. Installed through **npm or pip**? Update with your package manager on every platform (`npm install -g codebase-memory-mcp@latest` / `pip install -U codebase-memory-mcp`). ### Uninstall ```bash codebase-memory-mcp uninstall ``` Removes owned agent config entries, skills, hooks, instructions, and the installed binary. Existing graph indexes are listed and **kept by default**. `-y`/`--yes`, `-n`/`--no`, and noninteractive input keep them unless `--delete-indexes` is explicitly given. An interactive terminal without that flag is asked separately; the default answer is to keep them. ```bash codebase-memory-mcp uninstall -y --delete-indexes # also delete every project index codebase-memory-mcp uninstall --dry-run --delete-indexes # preview; change nothing ``` `--delete-indexes` is explicit consent and takes precedence over `--no`; `--dry-run` always preserves the files. When indexes are kept, uninstall prints their cache directory (`${CBM_CACHE_DIR:-~/.cache/codebase-memory-mcp}`) and how to remove them. The install script placed beside the binary is **reported, not deleted**: uninstall prints its path and the `rm` command for it. It is left alone on purpose: it may be your own copy, a symlink into a checkout, or managed by a package manager, and an uninstaller should not delete a file it cannot prove it owns. ## Features ### Graph & analysis - **Architecture overview**: `get_architecture` returns a compact summary by default. Request specific `aspects` for routes, hotspots, dependencies, clusters, or cycles. `system_structure` provides the projection used by CBM Lens and must be requested on its own. - **Architecture Decision Records**: `manage_adr` persists the project's decision record across sessions; indexing also extracts supported ADR metadata and supersession from documentation files - **Louvain community detection**: Discovers functional modules by clustering call edges - **Change impact**: `detect_changes` maps uncommitted changes to affected symbols with risk classification and can report test impact with `scope: "tests"`; `compare_graphs` compares indexed snapshots - **Runtime observations**: `ingest_traces` adds observed call relationships from separately collected traces alongside static analysis; static call paths alone do not show what ran - **Call graph**: Resolves function calls across files and packages (import-aware, type-inferred) - **Dead code candidates**: find functions with no indexed callers, excluding entry points. Check dynamic dispatch, coverage gaps, and framework conventions before removing code. - **Cypher-like queries**: `MATCH (f:Function)-[:CALLS]->(g) WHERE f.name = 'main' RETURN g.name` ### Search - **Semantic search** (the `semantic_query` parameter of `search_graph`, not a separate tool): vector search across the entire graph, powered by bundled Nomic `nomic-embed-code` embeddings (40K tokens, 768d int8) compiled into the binary; no API key, no Ollama, no Docker. 11-signal combined scoring (TF-IDF, RRI, API/Type/Decorator signatures, AST profiles, data flow, Halstead-lite, MinHash, module proximity, graph diffusion). - **BM25 full-text search** via SQLite FTS5 with `cbm_camel_split` tokenizer (camelCase / snake_case aware) - **Structural search** (`search_graph`): regex name patterns, label filters, min/max degree, file scoping - **Code search** (`search_code`): graph-augmented grep over indexed files only ### Documentation connected to code Find the explanation behind a symbol and follow supported references back to its implementation. Documentation participates in the graph alongside source files: - **Markdown, reStructuredText, and AsciiDoc** become navigable document sections; **PDFs with text layers** become searchable text pages. PDF extraction does not perform OCR. - **Document-to-code references** and supported language doc-comment references create `MENTIONS` relationships when the target can be resolved. - **Architecture decision records** contribute metadata such as status, deciders, and supersession, so decisions can be explored with the code they describe. - **Supported diagrams and OpenAPI descriptions** contribute structured entities. Extraction and reference resolution differ by format; not every textual mention becomes a graph edge. Use graph and text search to locate the relevant section, follow its recorded relationships, and open the source evidence. Check `check_index_coverage` before treating a missing result as proof that the repository has no such documentation or reference. ### Infrastructure and deployment Ask **"What deploys this service?"**, **"Which image runs it?"**, or **"Where does this configuration reach code?"** CBM connects supported infrastructure forms to the source they build, configure, and run: - **Containers and clusters**: Dockerfiles, Compose services, Kubernetes resources, Helm charts and releases, and Kustomize overlays and patches. - **Provisioning and configuration**: Terraform/OpenTofu resources and modules, tfvars overrides, Terragrunt dependencies, Ansible tasks and handlers, and supported configuration keys and environment-variable access. - **Build and delivery**: shell commands, Make targets, and supported CI steps that build images, invoke repository scripts, or deploy resources. For resolvable inputs, a trace can follow **Service → workload → image → Dockerfile → program**, or follow deployment and configuration relationships. Use `trace_path` modes for topology, deployment, and run paths. These are static relationships from supported source forms; dynamic values and unresolved templates can leave gaps. See [Edge types](#edge-types-selected) for the exact relationship rules and limitations. ### Cross-service linking - **HTTP** route ↔ call-site matching with confidence scoring - **gRPC, GraphQL, tRPC** service detection with protobuf Route extraction - **Channel detection** (`EMITS` / `LISTENS_ON`) for Socket.IO, EventEmitter, and generic pub-sub patterns across 8 languages with constant resolution ### Cross-repo intelligence - **`CROSS_*` edges** link nodes across multiple repos indexed under the same store - **Cross-repo architecture summary** combining services, routes, and dependencies across the indexed fleet - **Run status**: `index_status` (and the UI layout next to `linked_projects`) carries a `cross_repo` object, `{"status":"never_run"}` until `index_repository(mode="cross-repo-intelligence")` has run with that project as the source, then `"ran"` with `last_run_at`, `outcome`, `targets`, `projects_scanned`, `total_cross_edges` and `skipped_projects`. That is how you tell "never linked" apart from "linked, nothing matched". The status is stored in the project's own index next to its `CROSS_*` edges, so a reindex that rebuilds the index drops both at once and the status goes back to `never_run`. - **Skipped stores**: `target_projects: ["*"]` skips an index built before the #768 schema change rather than failing the whole run. The response lists each one as `skipped_projects: [{"name", "reason": "pre_768_schema", "hint": "reindex this project"}]`. ### Smart CI and test impact Use the graph to explain which tests a change reaches, and use that evidence to focus supported CI runs. **Smart CI is experimental** and has two layers: | Layer | What it does | What you supply | |-------|--------------|-----------------| | **CI job selection** | Chooses jobs from the changed-file list. | Repository-specific path and job rules; this repository's selector is an example. | | **Test selection** | Combines static reachability, changed tests, and admitted per-test coverage to select suites or tests. | A supported C/C++ test harness, configuration, a coverage map, and a runner that accepts named selections. | `codebase-memory-mcp test-impact select` produces a selection with reasons; `test-impact publish` produces the graph-and-coverage bundle used as its baseline. For agent-assisted investigation, `detect_changes` with `scope: "tests"` exposes test impact through MCP. **Narrowing currently supports C/C++ family code with this repository's test conventions or declared equivalents.** It is not general test selection for every language CBM indexes. Missing, stale, incompatible, or incomplete evidence broadens the selection or returns `run_all`; static reachability without admitted coverage never omits a suite. Begin with report-only shadow mode and validate your harness before enabling gating. In this repository, test narrowing is on for every PR unless `TEST_IMPACT_MODE` says otherwise: the Linux x86_64 test leg runs the selection, and the arm64, macOS and Windows legs run it with every platform-specific suite whole; release and dry-run workflows retain full execution. See the [Smart CI guide](docs/SMART_CI.md) for supported conventions, coverage admission, setup, version requirements, and fallback behavior. ### Edge types (selected) - `CALLS`: a callable is invoked at the source site - `CALL_REFERENCE`: a callable is used at a supported reference site (for example, a direct value argument) and resolves to one exact target - `USAGE`: an identifier is used, but a unique callable target is not proven (including ambiguous or complex expressions) - `IMPORTS`, `DEFINES`, `IMPLEMENTS`, `INHERITS` - `HTTP_CALLS`, `ASYNC_CALLS` (cross-service); a shell script, Make recipe or CI step running `curl` / `wget` on a URL it states (constant words resolved, unknown parts `{}`) to its `Route` with the method its flags give: a Kubernetes Service of the repository by the path, as code clients do, any other host (a download, localhost) with the host kept; the edge keeps `via`, `method`, `url_path`, `host`, never the user info or the query - `SPAWNS`: the caller starts another program (`subprocess.run`, `exec.Command`, `posix_spawn`, `Process.Start`, a shell command or Make recipe running a program by path, ...); the target is a `Process` node named after the program, or `` when the program is not a literal. When a shell script, Make recipe, GitHub Actions step or Prow job runs a script of the repository (`./hack/x.sh`, `bash hack/x.sh`), the target is that script's `Module` (else its `File`); `make TARGET` (also `$(MAKE)`, `-C`, `-f`) targets the rule of that target, followed through included makefiles; edges from CI carry `ci` and `job`. A Dockerfile's last stage `ENTRYPOINT` (else `CMD`) spawns what the container runs (`api: dockerfile`): the repository script or source copied into the image, the Go `main` of a binary a stage builds with `go build -o`, else a `Process` - `INFRA_MAPS`: a Kubernetes Service to each workload whose pod labels carry every `key: value` of the Service's selector, within one namespace - `CONNECTS_TO`: a Kubernetes workload or compose service to the Service its containers' environment addresses (`PRODUCT_CATALOG_SERVICE_ADDR: productcatalogservice:3550`, a URL's host, `..svc...`, a bare name on an `*_ADDR` / `*_HOST` / `*_URL` / ... key; compose: the project's `.env` interpolated): a Kubernetes Service of the same bundle and namespace, or a compose service of the same file. The edge keeps `via: env`, `key` and `container`, never the value - `USAGE` with `ref: image`: a Kubernetes workload (any pod template: containers, initContainers, CronJobs, custom resources) or a docker compose service to the `Image` it runs - Helm templates are rendered for their images: with the chart's values (the `Chart` `DEPLOYS` them, `default_of`: the values keys read) and with each release's (a Flux HelmRelease, a kustomize `helmCharts` entry, a Terraform `helm_release`: `override_of`). An image the render cannot know is left out, never guessed: after a change of values it does not run exactly, a `tpl` or include it cannot look into, a release value it cannot read, or a work budget it runs past. Known limit: each template file renders on its own, while Helm renders a chart's files with one shared `.Values` (a subchart's is its parent's `.Values.`), so a chart that changes `.Values` in one file and reads it in another can still show a wrong image - `DEPLOYS`: what puts manifests, kustomizations or charts on a cluster, to what it puts there: a Flux Kustomization or Argo Application to the kustomizations / manifests / chart of its path, a Flux HelmRelease to its chart (`spec.chart` or `chartRef` → OCIRepository), a shell command or Make recipe (`kubectl apply -f/-k`, `kustomize build | kubectl apply`, `helm install/upgrade/template`), a Go installer loading a chart with the Helm SDK, a Terraform `helm_release`, a Terraform `kubernetes_*` resource the object it declares (a `Resource` like a manifest's, `ecosystem: terraform`, when its name is a literal), a kustomization inflating a chart (`helmCharts`; its values file an `IMPORTS`). A chart outside the repository is an external `Chart`, keyed by its publisher when its repository URL is stated (`__chart__/`, the same node in every project, the URL in `repository`), else one per project and name; the edge says `via` (`flux`, `argo`, `helmrelease`, `kubectl`, `kustomize`, `helm`, `helm-sdk`, `terraform`, `helmcharts`, ...) - `DEPENDS_ON`: a Helm chart to the charts it declares (the local chart for a resolvable `file://` repository, otherwise an external `Chart`; the edge keeps `repository`), and a `go.mod` / `requirements.txt` file to an external `Package`; a Dockerfile to the `Image`s it builds on (`via: from`, `copy-from`); an `Image` to the Dockerfile it is built from (`via: build`; `tool`: `skaffold`, `compose`, `docker-build` for `docker` / `podman` / `nerdctl` / `buildah` build commands in scripts, Make and CI); a compose service to the services its `depends_on` / `links` name - `CONFIGURES`: code reading an environment variable to the shared `EnvVar` of that name (`strategy: env_access`); a Kubernetes container, compose service or Dockerfile (`ENV` of the image) setting one to that container's own `EnvVar` (`strategy: env_set`, with `source`: `value`, `configMapKeyRef`, `secretKeyRef`, `fieldRef`, ..., `compose`, `dockerfile`; values are never stored); and that container's `EnvVar` to the code reading the name inside the files its image is built from (`strategy: env_read`, with `dockerfile`): the image's files are the sources its Dockerfile's `COPY` / `ADD` put into it, less the context's `.dockerignore` - `CONFIGURES` with `strategy: key_symbol`: a code symbol to the config key it names (`config_key`). A YAML, JSON, HCL (Terraform, OpenTofu, tfvars), TOML or INI key links by exact name (`maxRetryCount` = `max_retry_count`) and only to code inside the config file's component: its directory, or the one around a `config/`, `configs/`, `conf/`, `settings/` or `etc/` directory. A `.env` or `.properties` key also links by substring (confidence 0.75) - `OVERRIDE` with `via: patch`: a Kustomize patch to each object of its kustomization's build it changes (child → base): a patch file's documents to the object of the same kind and name; an inline patch (from the kustomization) or a JSON6902 operation file to what its `target` selects (group, version, kind, name, namespace, label selector); a component's in the build of each kustomization including it. The edge keeps `kustomization`, `patch` and `line`; a patch file is an `IMPORTS` (`local_name: patches`) of its kustomization, never a member of the build - `OVERRIDE` with `via: namePrefix` / `nameSuffix`: an object a kustomization renames, from its variant: a `Resource` named with the deployed name (`capi-` + `controller-manager`; the prefixes of nested kustomizations outermost first, suffixes innermost first) in the namespace that build gives it, `ecosystem: kustomize`, which the kustomization's file `DEFINES`. CRDs, Namespaces and API services keep their names, as kustomize does. The edge keeps `kustomization` and `line` - `USAGE` with `via: terraform`: a Terraform / OpenTofu reference (`var.X`, `local.X`, `module.X`, `data.T.N`, `T.N`) from the top-level block holding it to the block of its module (the `.tf` / `.tofu` files of its directory) that declares it (a `locals` entry: its `locals` block); an entry of the block's `depends_on` list is a `DEPENDS_ON` instead. The edge keeps `ref` (`var`, `local`, `module`, `data`, `resource`) and `line`; a name only mentioned in string text is no reference. A module call with a local source (`module "net" { source = "./modules/net" }`) `IMPORTS` (`local_name`: the module's name) the `Folder` of that directory (the root directory: the `Project`), and `module.net.id` (also `module.net[0].id`, `module.net[*].id`) `USAGE`s (`ref: output`) the `output "id"` there, beside `module.net` - `OVERRIDE` with `via: tfvars`: a `.tfvars` assignment to a variable the module of its own directory declares, from the file's `Variable` to that `variable` block (the edge keeps `line`); a `.tfvars` file whose own directory declares none of its names sets the nearest ancestor module's that does, the edge marked `inferred` (such a file is applied by a `-var-file` the repository does not state) - Terragrunt (`via: terragrunt`): a unit (`terragrunt.hcl`), evaluated in its own context: an `include` `IMPORTS` (`local_name`) the file its `path` names; a `read_terragrunt_config` `IMPORTS` (`read`: the file holding the call) the file it names, from the block holding the call or, for a call in an included file, from the unit's `include` block that brings it in; a `dependency` `DEPENDS_ON` the other unit; a local `terraform` `source` `IMPORTS` its `Folder`. Paths may use `find_in_parent_folders`, `dirname` and `get_terragrunt_dir`; anything else is unknown and links nothing - Ansible (`via: ansible`): a playbook or task file (a YAML file whose top level is a sequence) `IMPORTS` (`local_name`: the directive) what its directives name: `import_playbook` a playbook, `include_tasks` / `import_tasks` / `include` a task file (from its directory, else its role's `tasks/`), `roles:` items and `include_role` / `import_role` a role's `Folder` (`roles/` at or above its directory). A templated target links nothing. Each task and handler is a `Function` (named by its `name:`, else its module; `source: ansible`, `kind`, `module`) that its file `DEFINES`: in a playbook's plays, a role's `tasks/` and `handlers/` files, and the files those include; a block's tasks, not the block. A `notify` `CALLS` (`via: notify`) each handler of that name or `listen` topic in the task's own role (else its file). A `kube` (kubespray's module) or `kubernetes.core.k8s` task `DEPLOYS` (`via: ansible`, `module`) the repository file its play rendered the applied manifest from: the `template` (in the role's `templates/`) or `copy` (its `files/`) task whose `dest` is the task's `filename`, item by item through `register` / `with_items` / `loop` lists the play states (a literal list, a `set_fact`, the role's `defaults` / `vars`), or a `k8s` `template:` argument - `EMITS`, `LISTENS_ON` (channels) - `DATA_FLOWS` with arg-to-param mapping + field access chains - `SIMILAR_TO` (MinHash + LSH near-clone detection, Jaccard scored) - `SEMANTICALLY_RELATED` (vocabulary-mismatch, same-language, score ≥ 0.80) ### Indexing pipeline - **164 vendored tree-sitter grammars** compiled into the binary - **Generic package / module resolution**: bare specifiers like `@myorg/pkg`, `github.com/foo/bar`, `use my_crate::foo` resolved via manifest scanning (`package.json`, `go.mod`, `Cargo.toml`, `pyproject.toml`, `composer.json`, `pubspec.yaml`, `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `mix.exs`, `*.gemspec`) - **Infrastructure-as-code indexing**: Dockerfiles (`Dockerfile.*`, `*.Dockerfile`, `Containerfile`: bases, what the container runs, `ENV`), container images (`Image`: the normalised repository, tag and digest on the edges; a repository built from several Dockerfiles, one per component tag, gets an `Image` per component), docker compose services (`Resource`), Kubernetes manifests (`Resource`, with `group`, `version`, `kind`, `namespace`, `labels` as `k=v,k2=v2`), Kustomize overlays (`IMPORTS` to their entries and patch files, `OVERRIDE` from their patches), Helm charts (`Chart`, `DEPENDS_ON`), Terraform / OpenTofu (`.tf`, `.tofu`, `.tfvars`) as graph nodes. A Service walks to the code it runs: Service → workload → `Image` → Dockerfile → `main` - **[Hybrid LSP semantic type resolution](#hybrid-lsp)** for Python, TypeScript / JavaScript / JSX / TSX, PHP, C#, Go, C, C++, Java, Kotlin, Rust, and Perl; a lightweight C implementation of language type-resolution algorithms, structurally inspired by and compatible with major language servers including tsserver / typescript-go, pyright, gopls, Roslyn, Eclipse JDT, and rust-analyzer (parameter binding, return-type inference, generic substitution, JSX component dispatch, JSDoc inference for plain JS files, namespace + trait + late-static-binding resolution for PHP, file-scoped namespaces + records + LINQ method syntax for C#, class-hierarchy + overload + lambda resolution for Java, extension-function + scope-function resolution for Kotlin, trait-method + UFCS resolution for Rust) - **RAM-first pipeline**: LZ4 compression, in-memory SQLite, single dump at end. Memory released after. ### Distribution & operation - **Native runtime set, zero infrastructure services**: SQLite-backed, persists to `~/.cache/codebase-memory-mcp/` - **Auto-sync**: Background watcher detects file changes in projects registered by active MCP sessions, including successful explicit `index_repository` targets, and re-indexes them automatically. - **Route nodes**: REST endpoints are first-class graph entities - **CLI mode**: `codebase-memory-mcp cli search_graph --project my-project --name-pattern ".*Handler.*"` - **Available on**: npm, PyPI, Homebrew, Scoop, AUR, `go install` ### Indexing modes | Mode | Use it for | |------|------------| | `full` | Full indexing with semantic analysis. This is the default. | | `moderate` | A filtered index with semantic analysis. | | `fast` | A filtered index without semantic analysis. | | `cross-repo-intelligence` | Link services across indexed projects, optionally limited by `target_projects`. | ## Team-Shared Graph Artifact Share a compressed graph snapshot so teammates can reuse an indexed baseline. `.codebase-memory/graph.db.zst` is a zstd-compressed snapshot of the knowledge graph that lives next to your source. The artifact is opt-in: `index_repository` writes it only with `persistence: true` (the default is `false`), and once it exists later indexes refresh it. Local indexes persist regardless. When a teammate indexes a clone with an existing artifact, CBM imports that baseline and applies their local changes incrementally. - **Format**: SQLite database, indexes stripped, `VACUUM INTO` compacted, then zstd 1.5.7 compressed (8 to 13:1 ratio typical) - **Two tiers**: - **Best** (`zstd -9` + index strip + `VACUUM INTO`); written by `index_repository` with `persistence: true` - **Fast** (`zstd -3`); refreshes an existing artifact on every other index, including the watcher's low-latency incremental updates - **Bootstrap**: when no local DB exists but the artifact is present, `index_repository` imports the artifact first, then runs incremental indexing, reusing the shared baseline where possible - **Merge policy**: the first export creates `.codebase-memory/.gitattributes` with `merge=ours`. Check your repository's Git merge-driver setup before relying on it for concurrent artifact updates. - **Commit it deliberately**: the artifact is rewritten on every index, including the watcher's Fast tier, and git stores each rewrite as a full new blob. Committing every refresh is what turns a 20 MB file into gigabytes of history; one team reached ~6 GB across ~350 commits of this single path. Pick a cadence (a release, a milestone, a nightly job) rather than committing every save. - **Git LFS, if it must move on every commit**: track it from the **repo-root** `.gitattributes` and leave the auto-created `.codebase-memory/.gitattributes` in place; the nearer file goes on supplying `merge=ours`, and only `filter` comes from the root: ```gitattributes .codebase-memory/graph.db.zst filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text ``` Track only the `.zst`; `artifact.json` is small and carries the schema version. The attribute applies to future commits only. Removing existing blobs requires a separate history migration. Two costs to weigh before adopting it: GitHub meters LFS storage and bandwidth, and its objects cannot be pruned without contacting support; and every teammate needs `git lfs install`; without it their checkout leaves a pointer file where the artifact should be, the integrity-checked import refuses it, and they fall back to a full reindex. - **Optional**: shared export is opt-in, and Git commits remain your choice. Add `.codebase-memory/` to `.gitignore` if you prefer everyone to reindex from scratch. The artifact provides a shared baseline while each developer keeps a local query database. ## How It Works codebase-memory-mcp is a **structural analysis backend**: it builds and queries the knowledge graph. The backend does not require a generative model. It relies on your MCP client (Claude Code, or any MCP-compatible agent) to be the intelligence layer. ``` You: "what calls ProcessOrder?" Agent calls: trace_path(function_name="ProcessOrder", direction="inbound") codebase-memory-mcp: executes graph query, returns structured results Agent: presents the call chain in plain English ``` With MCP, your coding agent translates a question into tool calls. CBM Lens can also use an optional browser model for explanations; this does not change how the backend indexes or queries code. ## Performance Published backend benchmarks on Apple M3 Pro. These are separate from the CBM Lens checks: | Operation | Time | Notes | |-----------|------|-------| | **Linux kernel full index** | **3 min** | 28M LOC, 75K files → 4.81M nodes, 7.72M edges | | Linux kernel fast index | 1m 12s | 1.88M nodes | | Django full index | ~6s | 49K nodes, 196K edges | | Cypher query | <1ms | Relationship traversal | | Name search (regex) | <10ms | SQL LIKE pre-filtering | | Dead code detection | ~150ms | Full graph scan with degree filtering | | Trace call path (depth=5) | <10ms | BFS traversal | **Memory-aware pipeline**: Indexing keeps hot data in memory and can spill extraction results to disk when needed. Memory is released back to the OS after indexing completes. **More focused context, fewer tokens**: The project's [31-repository preprint](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.27277v1#S4.SS1) reports **10× lower token use** and **2.1× fewer tool calls** compared with file-by-file exploration. These March 2026 backend measurements cover the study's workloads and agent setup; the paper documents the full evaluation. An earlier [five-query comparison](https://github.com/DeusData/codebase-memory-mcp/blob/4ff6feeab639c4668da0f491930326ed5ec63093/README.md#performance) reported ~3,400 versus ~412,000 tokens for structural queries. The study's [system-performance measurements](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.27277v1#S4.SS3) include the Linux indexing and Cypher timings above. Explore the [measurement guide](docs/MEASURING_SAVINGS.md) to evaluate quality, latency and token use on your own workload. ## Troubleshooting & Diagnostics codebase-memory-mcp **indexes and queries locally and collects no telemetry**. When you hit something we can't reproduce on our side (a slow memory climb over hours, a performance regression, a leak that only appears after days of real use), **we have no diagnostic data unless you choose to send it.** Here is how to capture it yourself. ### Capture a diagnostics log Set `CBM_DIAGNOSTICS=1` before the first daemon-backed MCP session starts, then reproduce the problem (let it run as long as it takes; a slow leak needs time to show in the trend). The shared daemon captures this setting from the session that starts it. If it is already running, close all daemon-backed sessions so it exits before changing the setting. The daemon creates a fresh owner-private `cbm-diagnostics--` directory below the system temp directory (`$TMPDIR` or `/tmp` on macOS/Linux, `%TEMP%` on Windows). The exact paths are recorded by the `diagnostics.start` event in `${CBM_CACHE_DIR}/logs/cbm-daemon.log`: | File | What it is | |------|------------| | `trajectory.ndjson` | **The memory trajectory**: one JSON line every 5 s with `rss`, `committed` (Windows commit charge), `peak_*`, `page_faults`, `fd`, and `queries`. **This is the file we need for memory/leak reports**: the *trend over time* is what pinpoints a leak. It is **kept on disk after the server exits** (so you can grab it post-mortem) and rotates to `trajectory.ndjson.1` past ~8 MB. | | `snapshot.json` | The latest snapshot only; handy for a quick live check. Removed on clean exit. | The private randomized directory prevents another local account from pre-placing a link or special file at a predictable diagnostics path. Its `` component is the shared daemon's process ID, also recorded by the `daemon.start` event. Set the variable consistently in the `env` block of each agent's MCP server config, or export it before launching the first session. ### What to share When you open a memory/performance issue, **attach the `.ndjson` trajectory**: it contains no source code or query text, only resource counters. If you'd rather not attach a file, paste it (or an agent's summary of it) into the issue: your assistant can read the NDJSON directly and report whether `rss`/`committed` grow monotonically, how fast, and relative to query count; which is exactly what we need to find the cause. ## Installation ### Pre-built Binaries | Platform | Archive | |----------|---------| | macOS (Apple Silicon) | `codebase-memory-mcp-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` | | macOS (Intel) | `codebase-memory-mcp-darwin-amd64.tar.gz` | | Linux (x86_64) | `codebase-memory-mcp-linux-amd64.tar.gz` | | Linux (ARM64) | `codebase-memory-mcp-linux-arm64.tar.gz` | | Windows (x86_64) | `codebase-memory-mcp-windows-amd64.zip` | Every release includes `checksums.txt` with SHA-256 hashes. ## Multi-Agent Support `install` configures **46 supported automatic/conditional client surfaces**: 40 detected automatically and 6 conditional or explicit. “Conditional” means the installer writes only when the documented platform or an explicit, already-existing config path proves the target is active. It never flips experimental feature flags, enables plugins, YOLO modes, global permission bypasses, or third-party instruction trust. Where a client has a documented custom-agent format, the installer creates three exact-owned definitions from one canonical contract: - **Scout (Tier 1)**: about 3 to 4 narrow calls for fast positive, provisional discovery; no absence, exhaustive-impact, or dead-code claims. - **Verify (Tier 2, default)**: task-directed graph evidence, exact source checks, path coverage for every cited file, and scope coverage before negative claims. - **Auditor (Tier 3)**: bounded scope, current index generation, complete relevant pagination, broader relationship checks, and explicit unresolved limitations. Every direct tier batches `check_index_coverage` for its evidence paths and reads flagged ranges or skipped/excluded files directly. A clean coverage result means only “no recorded gap,” never proof of completeness. Clients without safe child MCP access receive the same three tiers as parent-handoff agents; the parent must supply project, generation, pagination state, graph evidence, and coverage results.
